reference.source: Manson's Tropical Diseases; CDC parasitic disease guidance
clinicalPearls: A food-borne tissue nematode infection caused chiefly by Gnathostoma spinigerum, acquired by eating undercooked freshwater fish, eels, frogs, poultry or snakes
Endemic in Southeast Asia, notably Thailand, and increasingly reported from Latin America and among returning travellers
The hallmark is intermittent, migratory subcutaneous swellings that move over days, often with overlying erythema, itch or pain
Peripheral eosinophilia is common and supports the diagnosis in the right exposure context

The larva cannot mature in humans and wanders through tissues, so the most feared complication is invasion of the central nervous system causing eosinophilic meningitis, radiculomyelitis or haemorrhage
Serology helps confirm the diagnosis, as recovering the larva is uncommon
Treatment uses anthelmintics such as albendazole or ivermectin, sometimes with corticosteroids for the inflammatory reaction; surgical removal is possible if a migrating larva is accessible
A dietary history of raw or undercooked freshwater animal flesh is a key diagnostic clue
reference.pathophysiology: Human gnathostomiasis follows ingestion of third-stage Gnathostoma larvae in undercooked or raw intermediate hosts such as freshwater fish and other flesh. Humans are accidental hosts in which the larva cannot develop into an adult worm. Instead it penetrates the gut wall and migrates through the liver and other tissues, then wanders through the subcutaneous tissues and, less often, deeper structures. This migration provokes eosinophil-rich inflammation and produces the characteristic shifting swellings. Aberrant migration into the central nervous system causes tracking damage and haemorrhage, giving rise to eosinophilic meningitis and myeloradiculopathy that account for the most serious morbidity.
additionalDifferentials: Sparganosis and other migrating tissue helminths
Other causes of eosinophilic meningitis such as angiostrongyliasis
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film for eosinophilia
Cerebrospinal fluid examination (often eosinophilic, sometimes xanthochromic) if neurological involvement is suspected
MRI of the brain or spinal cord in neurological disease
Histology or identification of a larva if surgically retrieved
redFlags: Headache, radicular pain, limb weakness or altered consciousness suggesting central nervous system invasion
Signs of intracranial or spinal haemorrhage
reference.prognosis: Cutaneous disease is generally benign though it may relapse over months to years, whereas central nervous system gnathostomiasis carries a serious prognosis with a risk of permanent neurological deficit or death.
pitfalls: Not eliciting a history of eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish or other flesh
Attributing migratory swellings to allergy or angioedema
Failing to consider neurognathostomiasis in eosinophilic meningitis from an endemic area
Assuming a single course of anthelmintic guarantees cure, as relapse can occur
Overlooking the diagnosis in a returning traveller with eosinophilia
management: Treat cutaneous and visceral disease with anthelmintic therapy using albendazole or ivermectin
Physically remove or surgically extract the migrating larva when it is superficially accessible
Add corticosteroids to dampen the eosinophilic inflammatory response, particularly in central nervous system involvement
Provide supportive neurological care in eosinophilic meningitis or myeloradiculopathy, managing raised intracranial pressure and haemorrhagic complications
Advise avoidance of raw or undercooked freshwater fish, eels, frogs, poultry and snakes to prevent reinfection
Monitor eosinophilia and symptoms for relapse over months, and refer to infectious diseases or tropical medicine
